COMPREHENSIVE REPORT: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE PATENT ANALYSIS¶

ILLUSTRATED VERSION WITH DATA VISUALIZATIONS¶

Corrected Version - Complete Analysis¶

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY¶

This report presents findings from 13 detailed patent analyses of bacterial antibiotic resistance technologies, covering 3,717 unique patent families filed from 2000 onwards. Patents are legal documents that protect inventions - a "patent family" represents the same invention filed in multiple countries. This analysis examines:

  • Where these patents are filed
  • Who owns them
  • What technologies they cover
  • Their global impact
Back to top

A note on the different "total families" figures in this report NEW — added 2026-07-17

Sharp-eyed readers will notice this report quotes a few different totals for "the dataset": 3,974 (base search results), 3,717 (Executive Summary, SDG Mapping, Overall Conclusions), 3,716 (IPC/Technology Co-occurrence Network), and 3,585 (Technology Clustering). This is a demo/training report, not a client deliverable, so we're flagging this openly rather than papering over it.

These are not four different searches — they're the same underlying search, viewed through slightly different filters at different points in the original analysis:

  • 3,974 is the full result of the original keyword + IPC/CPC search (2000 onwards) — the base population everything else draws from.
  • 3,585 (clustering) is confirmed — by directly checking family IDs, not just comparing totals — to be a 100% subset of the 3,974: every single clustered family exists in the base dataset. It's smaller because clustering needs enough IPC signal to place a family meaningfully in feature space; families with too little classification data get dropped for that specific method, not excluded from the analysis generally.
  • 3,717 / 3,716 almost certainly follow the same pattern (both within 1% of 3,974, and only 1 apart from each other), but we can't point to the exact filter that produced them: the original notebook's code cells were fully removed when this report was exported, so the precise logic isn't recoverable from the file itself.

In short: the variation looks like normal, unremarkable data-completeness filtering across sub-analyses (some families lack a title, a usable IPC code for a specific method, etc.), not inconsistent or fabricated data. For a real client deliverable, we'd insist on one harmonized denominator throughout — here, given the demo purpose, we're just being transparent about why the numbers move around a little instead.

2b. Innovation Waves — Historical Context NEW — added 2026-07-16

Analysis 2 identifies five filing "waves" but doesn't connect them to external events. The timing lines up with several well-documented global antimicrobial-resistance (AMR) policy and scientific milestones — offered here as plausible context, not proven causation: patent counts alone cannot establish that any single event caused a given wave's filing volume.

Wave 1 (2000–2004, 1,079 applications, baseline): follows shortly after the WHO's first Global Strategy for Containment of Antimicrobial Resistance (2001), the earliest major coordinated international policy response to AMR.

Wave 2 (2005–2009, 1,220, +13.1%): steady growth alongside rising clinical alarm over MRSA and other hospital-acquired resistant infections across the US and Europe.

Wave 3 (2010–2014, 1,972, +61.6%): the sharpest acceleration coincides with the 2010 discovery of NDM-1 ("New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase"), which triggered global alarm over pan-resistant Gram-negative "superbugs" and renewed urgency in antibiotic R&D funding.

Wave 4 (2015–2019, 2,362, +19.8%, overall peak): the single peak filing year across the whole dataset, 2015 (573 applications), is the same year the WHO Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance was formally adopted at the World Health Assembly — a landmark international commitment that mobilized funding and coordinated R&D priorities worldwide.

Wave 5 (2020–2023, 1,399, -40.8%): the sharp decline coincides with the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2022), widely reported by WHO and antibiotic-pipeline trackers (e.g. the PEW Charitable Trusts) to have diverted global pharmaceutical R&D funding, clinical trial capacity, and regulatory attention away from antibiotic development.

4b. Triadic Patent Families NEW — added 2026-07-16

Triadic patent families — those with protection sought at all three major offices (EPO, USPTO, JPO) — are a standard proxy for an invention's perceived global commercial value: filing and prosecuting in all three jurisdictions is expensive, so applicants only do it for inventions they expect to matter internationally.

Using the existing 3,974-family dataset (Analysis 1), families with a granted or B-kind US publication were isolated as a triadic-strength proxy, then their applicants and countries of residence were retrieved directly from PATSTAT.

573

2,634

Leading country (949)

Country of Residence of Applicants (Triadic Families)

Key finding: the USA dominates triadic-strength antibiotic resistance patents (949 applicant instances), followed by Japan (205), China (123), South Korea (118), and France (112) — a pattern consistent with the broader geographic leadership already seen in Analysis 2, but concentrated among the players willing to pursue the most expensive, broadest protection.

OVERALL CONCLUSIONS¶

Based on Verified Data¶

1. 🌏 GEOGRAPHIC LEADERSHIP¶

China leads in antibiotic resistance patent filings with 2,232 national applications (27.8%), significantly ahead of the United States with 1,540 applications (19.2%). The Asia-Pacific region dominates with 51.2% of all national filings.

2. 📉 DECLINING TERRITORIAL PROTECTION¶

The data shows a dramatic 69.6% decline in applications per patent family from 2000-2005 (4.44 apps/family) to 2021-2023 (1.35 apps/family). Single-country filings increased from 47.5% to 86.2%.

This suggests:

  • Economic constraints (filing costs)
  • Lower commercial expectations
  • More selective filing strategies
  • Risk assessment favoring limited protection

3. ⚠️ LOW GRANT RATE¶

The actual grant rate is 40.37% (5,716 granted out of 14,160 applications), meaning MORE applications are rejected/abandoned (59.63%) than granted.

This indicates:

  • High patent office standards
  • Speculative or low-quality applications
  • High abandonment rate
  • Challenging patent landscape

4. 📊 INNOVATION MOMENTUM¶

Patent family creation peaked in 2015-2019 (2,362 applications), followed by a 40.8% decline in 2020-2023 (1,399 applications).

5. 🏛️ INSTITUTIONAL LANDSCAPE¶

Analysis of 4,456 unique applicants shows:

  • Individuals: 32.8%
  • Companies: 32.5%
  • Universities: 24.4%
  • Balanced innovation ecosystem

6. 🔬 TECHNOLOGY DIVERSITY¶

The dataset covers 130 unique IPC classes with 54,752 total classifications (14.7 per patent), spanning:

  • Pharmaceuticals (55%)
  • Diagnostics (34%)
  • Biotechnology (11%)

7. ⏱️ TEMPORAL EVOLUTION¶

  • Peak filing: 2015
  • Peak apps/family: 2008 (6.04)
  • Recent trend: More families, fewer apps per family
  • Geographic shift: China's rise to dominance

8. 🌍 GLOBAL IMPACT¶

Mapping to UN SDGs shows broad societal impact:

  • Health (98.1%)
  • Innovation (92.9%)
  • Food security (63.9%)
  • Water quality (26.9%)

9. ✅ DATA RELIABILITY¶

This report is based on executed analysis of PATSTAT database covering 3,717 unique patent families. All numbers are directly extracted from executed notebook outputs.

10. ⚠️ LIMITATIONS¶

  • Patent data only (excludes unpublished research)
  • Recent years may show incomplete data (publication lag)
  • Citation data has 3-5 year lag
  • Grant rates through 2023; recent apps still pending
  • Classification-based search limitations

KEY TAKEAWAYS FOR STAKEHOLDERS¶

🏛️ For Policy Makers¶

  • China leads antibiotic resistance patent filings
  • Declining territorial protection suggests reduced commercial confidence
  • Low grant rates (40.37%) indicate quality/examination challenges
  • Innovation continues but with selective geographic protection

🔬 For Researchers¶

  • 3,717 patent families = substantial global R&D investment
  • Technology spans 130 different classifications
  • Both commercial and academic institutions actively innovating
  • Multiple visualization files available for analysis

🏢 For Industry¶

  • Declining apps/family (-69.6%) may indicate market challenges
  • Single-country filings dominate (86.2% in 2021-2023)
  • Major pharma companies active but reduced scope
  • Strategic filing focused on key markets only

💼 For Investors¶

  • Innovation peaked 2015-2019, declined 40.8% recently
  • Low grant rate (40.37%) = high-risk landscape
  • Reduced territorial protection may signal lower returns
  • China market = largest opportunity (27.8%)
